Magadha: India. Magadha (IPA: [məɡəd̪ʰaː]) was a region and kingdom in ancient India, based in the eastern Ganges Plain.
In which country is History of Victoria?
History of Victoria: Australia. The history of Victoria refers to the history of the Australian state of Victoria and the area's preceding Indigenous and British colonial societies.
In which country is Battle of Passchendaele?
Battle of Passchendaele: Belgium. Passchendaele (now Passendale) lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 5 mi (8 km) from Roulers (now Roeselare), a junction of the Bruges-(Brugge)-to-Kortrijk railway.
In which country is History of Bangkok?
History of Bangkok: Thailand. The history of Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, dates at least to the early 15th century, when it was under the rule of Ayutthaya.
In which country is Battles of Narvik?
Battles of Narvik: Norway. Narvik provided an ice-free harbour in the North Atlantic for iron ore transported by rail from Kiruna in Sweden.

Tlatelolco massacre: Mexico. The event occurred ten days before the opening ceremony of the 1968 Summer Olympics, which were carried out as scheduled.

Kingdom of Württemberg: German. The elevation formed part of Napoleon’s broader policy of strengthening allied German rulers in return for political and military support.
Which of these is an official language of Islamic State?
Islamic State: Arabic. It is designated as a terrorist organisation by the United Nations and many countries around the world, including Muslim countries.
Which of these was an official language of the Khwarazmian Empire?
Khwarazmian Empire: Persian. The Khwarazmian Empire (English:), or simply Khwarazm, was a culturally Persianate, Sunni Muslim empire of Turkic mamluk origin, ruled by the Anushtegin dynasty.
Which country uses the Roman scudo as its official currency?

The Roman scudo is the official currency of Papal States. At their zenith, the Papal States covered most of the modern Italian regions of Lazio (which includes Rome), Marche, Umbria, Romagna, and portions of Emilia.
Briefly his country's first prime minister in 1960, he then served as its first president until 1982, knitting together the French- and English-speaking halves of Cameroon — who was he?
Ahmadou Ahidjo (24 August 1924 - 30 November 1989) was a Cameroonian politician who was the first president of Cameroon from 1960 until 1982.
This founder of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party also ran training camps for the Grey Wolves from 1968 to 1978 — who is he?
Alparslan Türkeş (Turkish; 25 November 1917 - 4 April 1997) was a Turkish politician, who was the founder and president of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) and the Grey Wolves (lk Ocaklar).
Before serving as a government minister overseeing sport and broadcasting, this four-time member of India's parliament led the country's cricket governing body from 2015 to 2017 — who is he?
Anurag Thakur (born 24 October 1974) is an Indian politician from the Bharatiya Janata Party and a Member of Parliament in the Lok Sabha from Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh.

The unexpected victory of vastly outnumbered English troops over the French on 25 October 1415 during the Hundred Years' War boosted English morale and lasted until 1429. What historic battle was this?
Battle of Agincourt ((t)) was an English victory in the Hundred Years' War. The Battle of Agincourt ( AJ-in-kor(t); French: Azincourt [azɛ̃kuʁ]) was an English victory in the Hundred Years' War.
Freddie Mercury built this 1975 Queen track from three songs he'd written, producing a chorus-less six-minute suite famous for its sudden operatic detour — which song is it?
Bohemian Rhapsody is a song by the British rock band Queen, released as the lead single from their fourth studio album, A Night at the Opera (1975).
Known for his land and agricultural reform initiatives, this Indian politician and independence activist served as prime minister for a mere six months, from July 1979 to January 1980. Who was he?

Charan Singh (23 December 1902 - 29 May 1987) was an Indian politician, peasant leader, author and an independence activist who briefly served as the prime minister of India from July 1979 to January 1980.

Sparked when Tsar Nicholas I demanded protection over the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects, this 1853–1856 conflict pitted Russia against an alliance of the Ottomans, France, Britain and Sardinia-Piedmont — what was it?

Crimean War was fought between the Russian Empire and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, the Second French Empire, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont from October 1853 to February 1856.

The granddaughter of the last ruling Maharaja of the princely state of Jaipur, this Bharatiya Janata Party politician has served as Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan since December 2023 — who is she?

Diya Kumari (born 30 January 1971) is an Indian politician from Bharatiya Janata Party currently serving as the Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan alongside Prem Chand Bairwa in the ministry of Bhajan Lal Sharma from 2023 December.
A longtime ally of Robert Mugabe and his first vice-president, this politician was dismissed only to seize power in a 2017 coup and has led Zimbabwe ever since — who is he?
Emmerson Mnangagwa (born 15 September 1942) is a Zimbabwean politician who has served as the president of Zimbabwe since 2017.
The CEO of the ACS engineering group, this Spanish businessman is better known as the football boss who launched the 'Galácticos' policy of signing the world's best players — who is he?
Florentino Pérez (Spanish; born 8 March 1947) is a Spanish businessman and the president of football club Real Madrid, as well as chairman and CEO of ACS Group, a civil engineering company.
At war's end in 1945, this German field marshal, who served as Commander-in-Chief in the West, was — at 69 with 52 years of service — the German Army's most senior officer. Who was he?

Gerd von Rundstedt (12 December 1875 - 24 February 1953) was a German Generalfeldmarschall (Field Marshal) in the Heer (Army) of Nazi Germany and Oberbefehlshaber West (Commander-in-Chief in the West) during World War II.
As a concubine of Selim I and mother of Suleiman the Magnificent, this woman became the very first to hold the empire's highest maternal title in the Ottoman court — who was she?
Hafsa Sultan (Ottoman; 1478/1479 - 19 March 1534), was a concubine of Selim I and the mother of Suleiman the Magnificent.
Encompassing Spaniards as well as Spanish-speaking populations in the Americas and beyond, this ethnic or meta-ethnic term traces back to lands once part of the Spanish Empire — what term?
Hispanic refers to people, cultures, or countries related to Spain, the Spanish language, or Hispanidad broadly.

Established after Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, inherited the West and Central Asian portion of the Mongol Empire, this successor state was officially known as the Land of Iran — what's the khanate called?
Ilkhanate was a Mongol khanate founded in the southwestern territories of the Mongol Empire.

Crowned King of Scotland at fifteen after his father fell in battle, this Stewart monarch built up the royal navy with 38 ships — including the Great Michael, the largest warship of its time — before dying at Flodden. Who was he?
James IV (17 March 1473 - 9 September 1513) was King of Scotland from 11 June 1488 until his death at the Battle of Flodden in 1513.

His signature on the Declaration of Independence was so large and stylish that his very name became American slang for one's autograph — which Founding Father, also the longest-serving president of the Continental Congress, left his mark?
John Hancock was American Founding Father (1737–1793).
This veteran Indian National Congress politician led Madhya Pradesh as Chief Minister from 2018 until a political crisis forced his resignation in 2020 — who is he?
Kamal Nath (born 18 November 1946; Hindi) is an Indian politician who served as the 18th Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh from 2018 to 2020 and resigned after a political crisis.
Serving as Deputy Marshal of Poland's Sejm and a member for both the League of Polish Families and later the Confederation, this far-right politician once chaired the All-Polish Youth — who is he?
Krzysztof Bosak (born 13 June 1982) is a far-right Polish politician.

This Germanic people migrated south from near present-day Hamburg, eventually conquering most of the Italian Peninsula in the late 6th century — a northern Italian region still bears their name — who were they?
Lombards were a Germanic people who conquered most of the Italian Peninsula between 568 and 774 AD.

This English princess became Queen of Scotland through marriage in 1503, later serving as regent for her young son — and her descendants eventually inherited the thrones of England and Ireland too — who is she?
Margaret Tudor (29 November 1489 - 18 October 1541) was Queen of Scotland from 1503 until 1513 as the wife of James IV.
As Director of Intelligence for the IRA during Ireland's War of Independence, this revolutionary later served as both Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Finance — who was he?

Michael Collins (Irish leader) (16 October 1890 - 22 August 1922) was an Irish revolutionary, soldier and politician who was a leading figure in the early-20th century struggle for Irish independence.
This Hebrew prophet led his enslaved people out of Egypt and, according to scripture, received a divine law that became part of the Torah — who is he?
Moses was the Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of slavery in the Exodus from Egypt.

This Florentine diplomat served Florence's republic while the Medici were out of power, then wrote a slim political treatise — unpublished until five years after his death — that earned him the title 'father of modern political science.' Who was he?
Niccolò Machiavelli (3 May 1469 - 21 June 1527) was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian who lived during the Italian Renaissance.

Living north of the Firth of Forth in early medieval Scotland, this group of peoples was likely descended from the Caledonii and other Iron Age tribes, and left behind carved memorial stones — who were they?
Picts were a group of peoples in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth, in the Early Middle Ages.

Succeeding the pharaoh who had stabilized Egypt at the end of the 18th Dynasty, this short-reigned ruler founded the 19th Dynasty and was father to one of ancient Egypt's most storied pharaohs — who is he?

Ramesses I was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt's 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292–1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295–1294 BC.
A leading theorist of Germany's SPD, she broke away to co-found the Spartacus League that became the KPD, and wrote influentially on imperialism and revolution — who is she?
Rosa Luxemburg (5 March 1871 - 15 January 1919) was a Polish and naturalised-German Marxist theorist and revolutionary.

Established in the early 20th century, this youth movement is built around practical outdoor skills like camping and woodcraft, and is symbolized worldwide by a fleur-de-lis insignia — what movement is it?
Scouting is a youth movement which became popularly established in the first decade of the 20th century.

Believed by most human cultures to be the immortal, immaterial essence of a living being distinct from the physical body, this concept is central to nearly every world religion and philosophy — what is it?
Soul is the immaterial aspect or essence of a living being. It is typically believed to be immortal and to exist apart from the material world.
Launched in January 1968 during a Lunar New Year holiday when most South Vietnamese troops were on leave, which surprise campaign became one of the Vietnam War's largest?
Tet Offensive was both a major escalation and one of the largest military campaigns of the Vietnam War.
Educated at Allahabad University, this Indian politician joined the Congress party in 1969 and later became prime minister for less than a year, from 1989 to 1990 — who is he?
V. P. Singh (25 June 1931 - 27 November 2008) was an Indian politician who served as the Prime Minister of India from 1989 to 1990 and the Raja Bahadur of Manda.

Fought between 1639 and 1653 across England, Scotland, and Ireland, this cluster of conflicts under Charles I climaxed in his execution and the birth of the Commonwealth of England — what's it called?
Wars of the Three Kingdoms is the collective term for a series of conflicts fought between 1639 and 1653 in England, Scotland and Ireland, then separate entities in a personal union under Charles I.
Fill in the blank: “____ is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti.”

Yoni is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti. Yoni (Sanskrit: योनि, IAST: yoni), sometimes called pindika, is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti.
An ethnic Uzbek warlord from Jawzjan province, he became a key ally of US Special Forces in the 2001 campaign to topple the Taliban and is nicknamed a 'kingmaker' of Afghan politics — who is he?
Abdul Rashid Dostum: Afghan politician and military officer (born 1954)
Once a rebel commander known by the nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Julani, he led the offensives that toppled the Assad regime and became president of Syria in 2025 — who is he?
Ahmed al-Sharaa: President of Syria since 2025. Al-Sharaa joined al-Qaeda in Iraq shortly before the 2003 invasion of Iraq and fought for three years in the Iraqi insurgency.

Serving in Lenin's 1917 government, this Russian revolutionary became the first woman in history to hold a cabinet post — and later among the first women appointed ambassador of a modern state. Who was she?
Alexandra Kollontai: Soviet politician and diplomat (1872–1952)
A co-author of the Russian Constitution, this legal scholar became the first democratically elected mayor of Saint Petersburg — who was he?
After her weaving skills provoked the wrath of Minerva in Ovid's telling, this mortal hanged herself in shame and was transformed into a spider -- who is she?
Arachne: Mythological weaver who was transformed into a spider.

Born in Somalia and granted asylum in the Netherlands at 23, this writer and activist entered Dutch centre-right politics after renouncing her childhood faith and identifying as an atheist — who is she?
Ayaan Hirsi Ali: Somali-born activist, politician, and author (born 1969)

He was the last Belgian king to be sovereign of the Congo, and in 2024 the Holy See opened the cause for his beatification — which childless monarch, who reigned from 1951 until his death, was succeeded by his younger brother Albert II?
Baudouin of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1951 to 1993.
In Buddhism, this term describes someone who has attained — or is working toward — enlightenment, often delaying their own nirvana to help others reach Buddhahood first. What is it?
Bodhisattva: Buddhist term for aspirant to enlightenment.
This Severan-dynasty Roman emperor seized sole power by having his brother Geta murdered by the Praetorian Guard — and is remembered by a nickname, not his birth name. Who was he?
Coaxed out of retirement in 1958, this French general commissioned a brand-new constitution that launched the Fifth Republic — then got himself elected its first president. Who was he?
Charles de Gaulle: French general and statesman (1890–1970)
Beginning after the Second World War and ending with the Soviet collapse in 1991, this rivalry never saw direct combat but did produce a Space Race — which conflict?
Cold War: 1947–1991 geopolitical rivalry between US and USSR.
The second woman ever to hold the job, after Dee Dee Myers, this commentator served as White House press secretary under George W. Bush before co-hosting Fox News's 'The Five' — who is she?
Dana Perino: American conservative political commentator (born 1972)
Rooted in a Sanskrit word meaning 'to hold or support,' this concept refers to one's moral duty and responsibility — a farmer's version differing from a soldier's — what's the term?
Dharma: Key concept in Indian philosophy and Eastern religions, with multiple meanings.
Also called the Great Patriotic War, this World War II theatre saw around 30 million deaths and is considered the main cause of Nazi Germany's defeat — what is it?
Eastern Front (World War II): Theatre of war of European Axis and Soviet Union blocs.
This revolutionary became the first president of an Asian constitutional republic, leading Filipino forces first against Spain and then against the United States — who was he?
This Israelite priest-prophet foretold Jerusalem's fall to the Neo-Babylonians in 587 BC and has an entire book of the Hebrew Bible named for him — who is he?
Ezekiel: Prophet in the Abrahamic religions.
Beginning with dukkha and moving through craving and its cessation, this Buddhist framework is described as 'how things really are when seen correctly' — what is it?
Four Noble Truths: Formulaic summary of Buddhist doctrines.
French politician born in 1989 who became the youngest and first openly gay prime minister in his country's history (January–September 2024). He now leads the Renaissance party. Who is he?
Gabriel Attal: Prime Minister of France in 2024. The snap election resulted in another hung parliament and electoral defeat for the government.
Serving as Italy's president from 2006 to 2015, this former Communist Party member became the country's longest-serving head of state and the first ever re-elected to the office — who was he?
Giorgio Napolitano: President of Italy from 2006 to 2015. In 2005, Napolitano was appointed a senator for life in Italy by then president Carlo Azeglio Ciampi.

In May 1980, student-led protests in a South Korean city rose against Chun Doo-hwan's coup and martial law, only to be crushed by the military at a cost of hundreds to thousands of lives — what is this event called?
Gwangju Uprising: 1980 anti-government protest in South Korea.
Formed in 2017 from a merger of Islamist factions, this group led the offensive that toppled the Syrian government in December 2024 — which organization?
Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham: Sunni Islamist and Jihadist military and political organisation.
This 3rd-century shamaness-queen ruled the land of Wa after decades of warfare, sending tribute to China's Cao Wei kingdom — who was she?
Himiko: 3rd-century Queen of Yamataikoku. Himiko (卑弥呼; c. 170–247/248 AD), also known as the Shingi Waō (親魏倭王; "Ruler of Wa, Friend of Wei"), was a shamaness-queen of Yamatai-koku in Wakoku (倭国).
Beginning with Napoleon's return from exile on Elba and ending with the second restoration of Louis XVIII after Waterloo, what name is given to this roughly 110-day period in 1815?
Hundred Days: 1815 period of the Napoleonic Wars.
The son of a former president and a lawyer by trade, he became the first holder of his nation's top office to have been born after its Declaration of Independence — which Israeli president?
Isaac Herzog: President of Israel since 2021.
This Royal Navy explorer led the first recorded European visit to Australia's east coast and the Hawaiian Islands, and circumnavigated New Zealand's main islands — who was he?
James Cook: British explorer and naval officer (1728–1779)

Originating from the Israelites and Hebrews of historical Israel and Judah in the Iron Age, the earliest mention of this people appears on the Merneptah Stele around 1213–1203 BCE. What is this history?
Jewish history: Jews originated from the Israelites and Hebrews of historical Israel and Judah, two related kingdoms that emerged in the Levant during the Iron Age.

This Polish statesman served as Chief of State after World War I and is regarded as the father of the Second Republic, re-established in 1918 after 123 years of partition. Who was he?

This semi-nomadic Turkic people built a major trading empire from the 6th century CE, dominating the Volga-Don steppes, Crimea, and the Caucasus for roughly three centuries as a crossroads on the Silk Road?
Khazars: Historical semi-nomadic Turkic ethnic group.

A founding member of the Organisation of African Unity, this Ghanaian revolutionary served as prime minister and then president of Ghana, and won the Soviet Union's Lenin Peace Prize in 1962 — who is he?
She led the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace movement that helped end the Second Liberian Civil War in 2003, sharing the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize — which Liberian activist is she?

Tracing itself back to a German friar whose push to reform the Catholic Church helped ignite the Reformation in 1517, this branch of Protestantism spells out its doctrine in the Book of Concord — what is it?
Lutheranism: Major branch of Protestantism. The Lutheran churches adhere to the Bible and the ecumenical creeds, with Lutheran doctrine being explicated in the Book of Concord.
Born in a village now in Pakistan and holding an Oxford doctorate in economics, this Indian leader was the country's first Sikh prime minister, serving from 2004 to 2014 — who is he?
Manmohan Singh: Prime Minister of India from 2004 to 2014. A member of the Indian National Congress, Singh was the first and remains the only Sikh prime minister of India.
Ruling for less than a year in 684–685, this fourth Umayyad caliph founded a new ruling house that held power until 750 — who was he?
Marwan I: Umayyad caliph from 684 to 685. Marwan later served as governor of Medina under his distant kinsman Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680), founder of the Umayyad Caliphate.
Denmark's youngest-ever prime minister, she became the second woman to hold the post when she succeeded Helle Thorning-Schmidt as party leader — who is she?
Mette Frederiksen: Prime Minister of Denmark since 2019.

Historians debate whether this era — born from the Renaissance and the Enlightenment — closed out by 1930, by 1945, or as late as the 1980s before giving way to a 'post' successor. What is the era called?
Modernity: Historical period and socio-cultural norm or attitude.
Founded in Egypt in 1928 by schoolteacher Hassan al-Banna, this Sunni Islamist group preaches 'Islam is the solution' and seeks a caliphate under Sharia — what is it?
Muslim Brotherhood: Transnational Sunni Islamist organization.
Founded by Pieter Omtzigt in 2023, this Christian-democratic party in the Netherlands is commonly known by the initials NSC — which party?
New Social Contract: Political party in the Netherlands.
Killed at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 and canonized a year later, this 'Eternal King of Norway' became a saint whose veneration helped spread Christianity among the Vikings — who was he?
Olaf Haraldsson: King of Norway from 1015 to 1028.

Established in the 8th century when the Frankish king Pepin the Short granted land to the pope, this Italian sovereign territory was ruled directly by the Church until Italian unification in 1870 — what was it?
Papal States: Italian state ruled by the pope (756–1870)
Inheriting his mother's Burgundian domains at just three years old, which Habsburg ruler became the first of his dynasty to be crowned king of Castile, in 1506?
Philip the Handsome: Habsburg ruler, King of Castile in 1506. Philip was the son of Maximilian I of Austria and Mary of Burgundy.
Founder of a Mumbai travelling theatre company in 1944, this actor became the patriarch of a Hindi-film dynasty spanning four generations — who is he?
Dubbed 'the greatest living explorer' in 1984, this baronet was the first person to reach both poles by surface travel and later summited Everest at age 65 — who is he?
This British Royal Navy officer reached the South Pole in January 1912, just five weeks after a Norwegian rival — but died with his men on the return journey — who was he?
Robert Falcon Scott: British Antarctic explorer (1868–1912)
The seventh adult man ever to embrace Islam, this military commander led the conquest of a Sasanian capital and founded the garrison city of Kufa — who is he?
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: Muslim general (c. 595 – 674)
Governor of five different Indian states over his career, this politician was serving as the final governor of Jammu and Kashmir when its special status was revoked in 2019 — who is he?
Known by the kunya Abu Idris, this Chechen guerrilla commander helped recapture Grozny in 1996 and later masterminded some of Russia's worst hostage-taking attacks — who is he?

After revealing Zeus's abduction of a nymph to a river god and later cheating death itself, this mythical king of Corinth was condemned to forever push a boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down — who is he?
Sisyphus: King of Ephyra in Greek mythology.
This Roman general became the first in the late Republic to march on Rome and win a civil war, later resigning his dictatorship after enacting constitutional reforms — who is he?
Sulla: Roman general and dictator (138–78 BC)
Rooted in shamanism and animism on the Eurasian steppes and centered on a sky god, this belief system was the state religion of the Mongol Empire — which one?
Tengrism: Religion of the Eurasian steppe nations.
Born in 1320, this ruler acceded to the throne in 1333 and became the last emperor of one dynasty and the first of its northern successor state after fleeing — who was he?
Toghon Temür: Emperor of Yuan dynasty from 1333 to 1368.
A trained physician who served as Germany's Defence Minister under Angela Merkel, she has led the European Commission since 2019 — who is she?
Ursula von der Leyen: President of the European Commission since 2019. Von der Leyen was born and raised in Brussels, Belgium, to German parents.
As Vice Chair of Russia's State Duma from a liberal-leaning party, he ran in the 2024 presidential election calling for peace negotiations 'without a rollback' — who is he?
Among Queen Victoria's 42 grandchildren he was the eldest, yet he'd preside over the end of his dynasty's 400-year grip on Prussia when he abdicated in 1918 — which last German Emperor?
Wilhelm II: German Emperor from 1888 to 1918.
This Indian politician, who leads the Andhra Pradesh unit of the Congress party, is the daughter of a former chief minister and younger sister of another prominent state politician — who is she?
This authoritarian ruler seized Tunisia's presidency in a bloodless 1987 coup by declaring his predecessor incompetent, then fled to Saudi Arabia when revolution toppled him in 2011 — who was he?
Zine El Abidine Ben Ali: President of Tunisia from 1987 to 2011.
Which of these people was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four. It is particularly useful in handling structured data, i.e., data incorporating relations among entities and variables.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Maria Goeppert Mayer is a physicist. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which of these is a chemist?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele is a chemist. Carl Wilhelm Scheele (German: [ˈʃeːlə], Swedish: [ˈɧêːlɛ]; 9 December 1742 – 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Livermorium?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
What is the atomic number of Polonium?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
In what year was Ferruccio Lamborghini born?
Ferruccio Lamborghini: In 1959, he opened an oil burner factory, Lamborghini Bruciatori, which later entered the business of producing air conditioning equipment.
In what year was Josef Mengele born?
Josef Mengele: Before the war, Mengele received doctorates in anthropology and medicine, and he began a career as a researcher.
In what year did Michael Rockefeller die?
Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.
In what year did Arthur Schopenhauer die?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 – 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
In what year did Ludwig Wittgenstein die?
Ludwig Wittgenstein: Wittgenstein was born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families.
In what year was Calcium discovered?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
Which company manufactures Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet?
Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: McDonnell Douglas. The Super Hornet is in service with the armed forces of the United States, Australia, and Kuwait.
Which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 from?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Soviet Union. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.
Who is credited with discovering Molybdenum?
Molybdenum: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
Who is credited with discovering Serotonin?
Serotonin: Arda Green. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
Who is credited with discovering Beryllium?
Beryllium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Stretching from the thoracic diaphragm to the pelvic brim, this body region sits between the chest and the pelvis — which body part?
Abdomen (also belly or stomach in vertebrates, or metasoma in arthropods) is the front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and in other vertebrates.

This Austrian psychotherapist founded a school of psychology emphasizing birth order and belonging, breaking from Freud by proposing that contributing to others is key to a person's sense of worth — who is he?
Alfred Adler (Austrian; February 7, 1870 - May 28, 1937) was an Austrian medical doctor, psychotherapist, and founder of the school of individual psychology.
Its scientific name translates roughly to 'fused lizard,' and it may be the largest of its armored kind at up to 8 tons — which dinosaur genus?
Ankylosaurus is a genus of armored dinosaur. It was named by Barnum Brown in 1908; it is monotypic, containing only A. magniventris.

Around 1920, when the energy source of stars was a complete mystery, which English astrophysicist boldly and correctly guessed it was the fusion of hydrogen into helium — and lent his name to a natural ceiling on a star's brightness?
Arthur Eddington (28 December 1882 - 22 November 1944) was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.
Coming on over about 48 hours, this temporary one-sided facial paralysis of unknown cause can droop an eyebrow, alter taste, and make sounds painfully loud — what is it?
Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.
In service with the U.S. Air Force since 1955 — and flown by NASA until 2007 — this subsonic strategic bomber can haul 70,000 pounds of weapons nearly 8,800 miles without refueling. Which aircraft?
Boeing B-52 Stratofortress is an American nuclear-capable subsonic jet-powered strategic bomber.
This Indian physicist discovered, with his student, that light changes wavelength when passing through a transparent material — a phenomenon now named for him — earning a 1930 Nobel Prize. Who is he?
C. V. Raman (7 November 1888 - 21 November 1970) was an Indian physicist known for his work in the field of light scattering.
A flightless ratite native to the tropical forests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia, this large bird has three living species and lacks a keel on its breastbone — name the bird?
Cassowary (Tok) are flightless birds of the genus Casuarius, in the order Casuariiformes.
Made of DNA wound around histone proteins, this substance shapes chromosomes into their distinctive forms during cell division and gatekeeps access to genes for transcription and repair — what is it?
Chromatin is a complex of DNA and protein responsible for condensing and packaging chromosomal DNA.
With algorithms and data structures at its core and the theory of computation among its branches, which field studies computation, information, and automation?

Computer science is the study of computation, information, and automation. The theory of computation concerns abstract models of computation and general classes of problems that can be solved using them.
Named after the bladder it was first found in, which amino acid carries a thiol side chain that forms the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together?
Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HSCH2CH(NH2)COOH.
Domesticated over 14,000 years ago — before farming even began — this descendant of wolves shares a common ancestor with the modern gray wolf. What animal is it?
Dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves.
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of her country's central bank, and was ranked among Forbes' most powerful women in 2019 — who is she?
Elvira Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
This term describes the practice of exposing normally covered body parts to others in public or semi-public settings, whether in person or via a nude photo shared digitally — what is it?
Exhibitionism is the practice of exposing one's intimate parts - such as the breasts, genitals, or buttocks - in a public or semi-public environment.
Sharing the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Maurice Wilkins, this English molecular biologist helped decipher the structure of DNA — who is he?
Francis Crick (8 June 1916 - 28 July 2004) was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist.

Built from epithelial tissue with a supporting connective-tissue capsule, this kind of structure secretes hormones straight into the blood if it's ductless, or through a duct to a cavity or surface if not — what is it called?
Gland is a cell or an organ in an animal's body that produces and secretes different substances that the organism needs, either into the bloodstream or into a body cavity or outer surface.

This British businessman and adventurer, chairman of a Dubai-based aircraft brokerage, visited the South Pole multiple times and descended to the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep before dying in 2023 when a submersible imploded in the North Atlantic - name him?
Hamish Harding (24 June 1964 - 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Domesticated in Central Asia around 4000 BCE, this one-toed hoofed mammal evolved over 45 million years from the small, multi-toed Eohippus — what is it?
Horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal.

Co-creator of the breakthrough neural network AlexNet and a contributor to landmark AI systems including GPT and AlphaGo, this computer scientist has won a major deep-learning research award three years running — who is he?
Ilya Sutskever (born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.
An economist-turned-pundit who rose to fame on Argentine TV talk shows, who became the nation's 57th president in 2023 under the banner La Libertad Avanza?
Javier Milei (born 22 October 1970) is an Argentine politician and economist who has served as the 57th president of Argentina since 2023.
This anesthetic drug induces a trance-like dissociative state while preserving breathing, and its S-enantiomer is now used to treat depression — name it?
Ketamine is a cyclohexanone-derived general anesthetic and NMDA receptor antagonist with analgesic and hallucinogenic properties, used medically for anesthesia, depression, and pain management.
With about 180,000 described species — roughly 10% of all known living organisms — which insect order is the second largest, trailing only the beetles?
Lepidoptera are an order of winged insects which include butterflies and moths.
This programming language, whose bytecode interpreter is written in ANSI C, was created in 1993 mainly to let developers extend and customize software — which language?
Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Known by a nickname, this Swedish programmer created Minecraft, the best-selling video game in history, and founded the studio Mojang in 2009 — who is he?
Markus Persson (born 1 June 1979), known by the pseudonym Notch, is a Swedish video game programmer and designer.
This Cuban engineer-turned-politician became his country's top leader in 2021, making him the first head of Cuba since the 1959 revolution who isn't a member of the Castro family — who is he?

Miguel Díaz-Canel (Latin American; born 20 April 1960) is a Cuban politician and engineer who has served as the 8th First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba and the top leader of Cuba since 2021.

Chemically known as bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, this organosulfur compound is a potent alkylating agent and carcinogen with no preventive antidote — protection relies entirely on covering the skin and airways. Name this notorious chemical warfare agent?
Mustard gas are names commonly used for the organosulfur chemical compound bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, which has the chemical structure S(CH2CH2Cl)2, as well as other species.
Catalyzed in nature by iron-bearing nitrogenase enzymes and famously partnered with legumes, this process turns molecular N2 into ammonia — what's it called?
Nitrogen fixation is a chemical process by which molecular dinitrogen (N2) is converted into ammonia (NH3).
The heaviest living bird, this flightless African species can sprint at 70 km/h and lays the largest eggs of any land animal on Earth — what bird is it?
Favored by royalty in the Chinese Imperial court, this toy dog breed originated in China's ancient capital — name the breed?
Pekingese (also spelled Pekinese) is a breed of toy dog, originating in China.
When this domesticated mammal reached Europe from the Near East, it interbred so freely with local wild boar that scholars still argue whether it's a distinct species — what animal is it?
Pig (Sus domesticus), also called swine (pl.: swine) or hog, is an omnivorous, domesticated, even-toed, hoofed mammal.
A staple food across the world, this tuber is actually an underground stem from a plant in the nightshade family, with wild relatives growing from the southern U.S. all the way to Chile. What is it?
Potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world.
Its common side effects read like a list of trade-offs — sedation, weight gain, dry mouth — yet many take this atypical antipsychotic simply to fall asleep — which medication?
Quetiapine (kwi-), sold under the brand name Seroquel among others, is an atypical antipsychotic medication used in the treatment of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder.
Holding a professorship in biology, neurology, and neurosurgery at Stanford, this primatologist is also a research associate with Kenya's National Museums — who is he?
Robert Sapolsky (born April 6, 1957) is an American academic, neuroscientist, and primatologist.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes patches of thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers in cold weather, with one severe subtype called CREST syndrome — what condition is it?
Scleroderma is a group of autoimmune diseases that may result in changes to the skin, blood vessels, muscles, and internal organs.
The brightest star in the night sky, this star sits in the constellation Canis Major and is actually a binary system paired with a faint white dwarf companion — name the star?
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, located in the southern constellation of Canis Major.
This round, gram-positive germ lives harmlessly on most people's skin and noses, but turn opportunistic and it triggers abscesses, sinus infections, and food poisoning. What is it?

Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive spherically shaped bacterium, a member of the Bacillota, and is a usual member of the microbiota of the body, frequently found in the upper respiratory tract and on the skin.
Its Latin species name vulgare simply means 'common,' yet this Asteraceae-family perennial turned invasive after spreading from Europe and Asia to Australia and the Americas — which plant?
Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) is a perennial, herbaceous flowering plant in the genus Tanacetum in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
This viral brain infection, transmitted through the bite of infected parasitic arachnids, saw its European case count climb almost 400% over three decades. What is this arachnid-spread illness?
Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a viral infectious disease involving the central nervous system, transmitted by the bite of several species of infected ticks.
This broad category of large, hoofed mammals was reclassified in 2001 into a new clade after genetic data revealed the older grouping wasn't a true evolutionary lineage. Name the category of animals?
Ungulate are members of the diverse clade Euungulata, which primarily consists of large mammals with hooves.
This unit of time, equal to seven days, serves as the standard calendrical period between a day and a month in most of the world. What is it?
Week (in the Western and international context) is a unit of time equal to seven days.
First synthesized by chemist Alexander Shulgin in 1974, this psychedelic compound produces hallucinogenic effects considered milder than LSD or psilocybin — what is it commonly known as?
2C-B: Psychedelic drug. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.
Also known as the buckeye or conker tree, this deciduous flowering tree is often confused with the unrelated sweet chestnut — which species?
Aesculus hippocastanum: Species of tree in the soapberry family.
Named for its carbon-carbon double bond, this class of hydrocarbon includes terminal versions known as alpha-olefins — what's the general term for it?
Alkene: Hydrocarbon compound containing one or more C=C bonds.
This group of diseases occurs when misfolded proteins accumulate in body tissue, causing fatigue, swelling, and shortness of breath among roughly 36 distinct protein-driven types — what is it?
Amyloidosis: Metabolic disease involving abnormal deposited amyloid proteins.
Originating from the heart's left ventricle, this is the largest artery in the human body, eventually splitting into the two common iliac arteries in the abdomen — what is it?
Aorta: Largest artery in the human body. The aorta distributes oxygenated blood to all parts of the body through the systemic circulation.
About 200 times sweeter than table sugar, this artificial sweetener sold as NutraSweet and Equal had its FDA approval briefly revoked before being re-approved in 1981 — what is it?

Once the go-to sedatives and anticonvulsants, these barbituric-acid-derived depressants were largely replaced by benzodiazepines and 'Z-drugs' because of their high addiction and overdose risk — what class of drugs?
Barbiturate: Class of depressant drugs derived from barbituric acid.
Produced continuously by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, this yellow-green fluid is released into the small intestine to help digest fats — what is it?
Bile: Dark greenish-brown fluid aiding in the digestion of fats.
Named for a Native American people of Oregon and Washington, this tandem-rotor heavy-lift helicopter grew out of Vertol's 1957 Model 107 design — what aircraft is it?
Boeing CH-47 Chinook: American tandem-rotor helicopter introduced in 1962 during the Cold War.
This group of roughly 20,000 non-vascular land plant species — liverworts, hornworts, and mosses — reproduces by spores instead of flowers or seeds. What is it called?
Bryophyte: Terrestrial plants that lack vascular tissue.
Once used in Italy for hunting large game and herding cattle, this mastiff breed today mostly serves as a guard dog or companion — which breed?
Cane Corso: Italian breed of mastiff. It is usually kept as a companion dog or guard dog; it may also be used to protect livestock.
Marked by patients who may lie motionless for days or repeat purposeless movements, this neuropsychiatric syndrome often responds to benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy — which condition?
Domesticated from the red junglefowl roughly 8,000 years ago, this bird now numbers over 26 billion worldwide, more than any other domesticated species — what is it?
Chicken: Domesticated subspecies of red junglefowl. The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) is the domesticated form of the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), originally native to Southeast Asia.
Native to the Indonesian island that gave part of its scientific name, this legume flower also goes by butterfly pea or blue pea — what is it?
Its species name honors Colchis, an ancient region on the Black Sea, and it's often released into the wild as a game bird — which Asian-native, ring-necked bird is this?
Common pheasant: Species of bird. The common pheasant (Phasianus colchicus), ring-necked pheasant, or blue-headed pheasant, is a bird in the pheasant family (Phasianidae).
Broken down from creatine phosphate in muscle metabolism, this compound is released into the blood at a rate tied to a person's muscle mass — what is it?
Creatinine: Breakdown product of creatine phosphate.
Also called thornapple or devil's trumpet, this genus of nine highly poisonous nightshade plants lent its American name to an outbreak in colonial Jamestown — what genus is it?
Datura: Genus of poisonous, potentially psychoactive plants.

This colourless, water-mixable lab solvent is technically odorless — but degraded samples reek of fish thanks to a dimethylamine impurity. It's better known by a three-letter abbreviation; what's the compound?
Dimethylformamide: Chemical compound. Dimethylformamide, DMF is an organic compound with the chemical formula HCON(CH3)2.
This German-born British economist championed 'human-scale, appropriate technology' in his 1973 book, later ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II — who was he?
E. F. Schumacher: British statistician and economist (1911–1977)
This messenger network of hormone feedback loops releases chemicals from internal glands like the thyroid, pituitary, and adrenal glands straight into the bloodstream to regulate distant organs?
Endocrine system: Hormone-producing glands of a body.

A women's-rights campaigner schooled in 1830s New York, she was the first scientist to show certain gases trap heat — anticipating that rising CO2 could warm the climate. Who was this overlooked pioneer?
Eunice Newton Foote: American scientist and activist (1819–1888)
This subfamily of cats, distinguished by a bony hyoid that lets its members purr instead of roar, is informally known as the small cats — which subfamily?
Felinae: Subfamily of Felidae. The Felinae or small cats are a subfamily of the Felidae distinguished by a bony hyoid, because of which they can purr but not roar.
This infection and inflammation of hair follicles produces pimples with white tips anywhere on hair-covered skin — what is the condition called?
Folliculitis: Human and animal disease of follicles.
Once classified under two different bacterial genera, this nonmotile coccobacillus forms small gray colonies on chocolate agar and has its own colistin-oxolinic acid selective medium — which species?
Gardnerella vaginalis: Species of bacterium. Gardnerella vaginalis is a species of Gram-variable-staining facultative anaerobic bacteria.
Nicknamed the blue dragon, this pelagic sea slug floats upside down using surface tension and a stomach gas bubble, and feeds on the Portuguese man o' war — what is it?

Nicknamed for its mole-like digging forelegs and dense fur, this insect widespread across Europe and introduced to the eastern United States is a textbook example of convergent evolution — which species?
Gryllotalpa gryllotalpa: Species of cricket-like animal.

Formally described only in 1983, this helical, flagella-driven bacterium burrows through the stomach's mucous lining and is the chief culprit behind gastric ulcers and some stomach cancers. What is it?
This extinct archaic human was the first to evolve a humanlike body and gait, the first to leave Africa for Asia and Europe, and the first to wield fire — who were they?
Homo erectus: Extinct species of archaic human. Homo erectus ( lit. 'upright man') is an extinct species of archaic human from the Pleistocene, spanning nearly 2 million years.

In this heart condition, the muscle walls, especially the wall between the ventricles, thicken without an obvious cause, weakening the heart's pumping and sometimes disrupting its electrical signals — which condition?

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Enlargement of the heart muscle. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM, or HOCM when obstructive) is a condition in which muscle tissues of the heart become thickened without an obvious cause.
Covering patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets, this legal category of intangible creations first developed as a concept in 17th- and 18th-century England — what is it called?
Intellectual property: Ownership of creative expressions and processes.
Caused by a buildup of bilirubin, this condition turns the skin and eyes yellowish and affects an estimated 80% of newborns in their first week of life — what is it?
Jaundice: Abnormal yellowish skin colour caused by high level of bilirubin.
This genus of coniferous trees and shrubs in the cypress family includes a species that forms the world's highest-known forest, at 4,900 metres in the Himalayas — what is it called?

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'hump,' this abnormal, excessive curving of the upper spine can result from osteoporosis, disc disease, or a condition common in teens called Scheuermann's disease — what is it called?
Kyphosis: Excessive convex curvature of the lower and middle spine.
Often beginning in the bone marrow, this group of cancers floods the body with immature 'blast' cells, bringing easy bruising, bone pain, and frequent infections — what is it?
Predominantly black and white with pink and grey highlights, this small Eurasian bird forms social flocks of six to seventeen outside breeding season and often nests in thorny scrub. What is it?
Long-tailed tit: Species of bird in Europe and Asia.

Discovered in 2005 by the same Palomar team whose haul of big, icy Kuiper-belt bodies pushed astronomers to demote Pluto in 2006, this fourth-largest dwarf planet has a methane-frosted, tholin-reddened surface — what is it?
Makemake: Dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Powered by two rear-mounted engines under a T-tail and fitted with built-in airstairs, this twin-engine jetliner entered service with Delta Air Lines in December 1965 — which aircraft is it?
McDonnell Douglas DC-9: Jet airliner, produced 1965-1982.
Used to treat nausea, vomiting, and gastroparesis, this dopamine receptor antagonist is also prescribed for migraines and appears on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Metoclopramide: Medication. It is thus rarely recommended that people take the medication for longer than twelve weeks.

An Egyptian-born civil engineer and architect who studied in Cairo and Germany, at 33 he was the oldest of the 19 hijackers and the ringleader who piloted American Airlines Flight 11 into the North Tower — who was he?
Mohamed Atta: Egyptian terrorist and 9/11 hijacker (1968–2001)
One of the smallest self-replicating organisms known, this cell-wall-lacking bacterium was originally called the 'Eaton agent' after being cultivated in chicken eggs in 1944 — what organism is it?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a species of very small-cell bacteria that lack a cell wall, in the class Mollicutes.
This British-American historian, a senior fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution, writes on financial history and holds notably favorable views of the British Empire — who is he?

This family within the superfamily Delphinoidea includes species with 'whale' in their common names, like the pilot and false killer types, and ranges up in size to the massive orca — what is this family called?
Oceanic dolphin: Family of marine mammals.
This genus of highly sociable ruminants includes domestic sheep, believed to descend from the wild mouflon of central and southwest Asia — which genus?
Ovis: Genus of mammals. Ovis is a genus of mammals, part of the Caprinae subfamily of the ruminant family Bovidae.
This Austrian theoretical physicist, who befriended Einstein in Prague in 1912 and later hosted him often in Leiden, lent his name to a theorem and key work on phase transitions — who was he?
Structurally related to a calming brain chemical and acting like baclofen or GHB on the same receptor, this anxiety medication can also give a mild dopamine-driven lift at low doses — what is it?
Caused by HPV and appearing on the sole of the foot with tiny black dots visible on its surface, this painful skin growth is treated with salicylic acid or freezing — what condition is it?
Plantar wart: Medical condition. A plantar wart, also known as a verruca, is a wart occurring on the bottom of the foot or toes.
Diagnosed only when symptoms like bloating, mood swings, and irritability disrupt daily life in the week or two before a period and resolve once it begins — what's this condition called?
Premenstrual syndrome: Emotional and physical symptoms that occur one to two weeks before a menstrual period.
This water-soluble organic compound, made of two fused rings, gives its name to a class that includes DNA's adenine and guanine bases — what is it?
Named for the way light stretches toward longer wavelengths, this phenomenon comes in Doppler, gravitational, and cosmological forms and is measured by the value z — what is it?
Redshift: Change in wavelength of light.
This British economist, who won the 1991 Nobel and spent decades at the University of Chicago Law School, urged the field to study real-world wealth creation in Adam Smith's spirit — who was he?
Ronald Coase: British economist and Nobel laureate (1910–2013)
First known as a portrait painter, this American inventor helped develop a single-wire telegraph system and lent his name to the dot-and-dash code introduced in 1837 — who is he?
Samuel Morse: American inventor and painter (1791–1872)
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, this term for a lucky accidental discovery describes how penicillin, Post-it Notes, and the microwave oven all came about — what is it?

Named in 1842 from Brazilian fossils and often called a saber-toothed tiger despite no close kinship to true tigers, this genus of prehistoric predator roamed the Americas until the early Holocene — which animal?
Smilodon: Extinct genus of saber-toothed cat.
With eight arms plus two extra tentacles for grabbing prey, this soft-bodied mollusc has an internal chitin rod called a gladius instead of a true skeleton — what creature is it?

A retired US Navy captain, this NASA astronaut became the first woman to fly on an orbital spacecraft's test flight in 2024 and had her ISS stay extended by more than nine months due to technical issues — who is she?
Sunita Williams: U.S. Navy officer and NASA astronaut (born 1965)
A math prodigy who abandoned academia in 1969 for a reclusive cabin life, the 'Unabomber' mailed bombs for 17 years and published a 35,000-word anti-technology manifesto — who was he?
Known commonly as garden thyme or German thyme, this flowering plant belongs to the mint family — which species is it?
Thymus vulgaris: Species of flowering plant.
This condition involves a long-term urge to pull out one's own hair, most often from the scalp or around the eyes, and is more common among those with OCD — what is it?
